Alex / team — technical notes below to inform the redline:

1) Backups & snapshots: For EU-hosted and private VPC deployments we store backups as encrypted snapshots in region-specific object storage. There are two categories:
   - Automated daily snapshots (retention by default 14 days)
   - Long-term backups (customer configured; used for restore/DR, typically 90 days)

We can guarantee the following operational commitments in the DPA:
   - Primary customer data will be deleted within 48 hours after a validated deletion request (subject to in-flight requests completion).
   - Automated snapshots will be destroyed and rendered unrecoverable within 30 days.
   - Long-term backups will be destroyed within 60 days unless the customer has explicitly requested retention.

2) On-prem / Private deployment nuance: If the customer requests an on-prem transfer of a dataset, we will coordinate a secure handoff. Once the customer confirms receipt, Redwood will perform the deletion procedure in the customer-controlled environment — this typically involves HSM-backed key destruction for encrypted data and NIST-compliant wipe where hardware access is provided. For cloud-hosted snapshots owned by Redwood, we must perform deletions and provide declaration of completion.

3) Audit evidence: We can produce a deletion declaration (signed PDF) that includes snapshot IDs, timestamps, and proof of key shredding where applicable. For SaaS (hosted) customers this will be our standard output; for on-prem we will include a checklist and acceptance signature.

Operational risk: the 30/60-day windows above are achievable but require coordination on the customer's side (acknowledgement of handoff, window for log export). If Acme insists on a 7-day absolute deletion for long-term backups, that will require re-architecting snapshot retention and may increase cost.

I'll draft Option A/Option B language for legal review.

Marta — thanks again. Please find two proposed redline snippets below (we can slot either into Section 4.2 / Section 6.1):

Option A (standard, lower risk):
"Upon Customer's validated deletion request or expiration/termination of the Agreement, Redwood will delete Customer Data in primary storage and related metadata within forty-eight (48) hours. Automated snapshots and short-term backups will be rendered unrecoverable and purged within thirty (30) calendar days. Long-term backups will be purged within sixty (60) calendar days unless Customer has submitted a written request to retain such backups. Redwood will provide a Deletion Declaration that includes affected snapshot identifiers and deletion timestamps. Customer shall have a fourteen (14) day window following termination to request export of logs and data prior to permanent deletion."

Option B (accelerated, higher cost):
"Upon Customer's validated deletion request or expiration/termination of the Agreement, Redwood will delete Customer Data in primary storage and related metadata within twenty-four (24) hours. All automated snapshots and backups will be purged within fourteen (14) calendar days. Redwood will provide a Deletion Declaration and, where applicable, evidence of cryptographic key destruction. Any customer-requested on-prem handoff must be acknowledged in writing; Redwood will perform asset/backup destruction within seven (7) calendar days of documented receipt confirmation."

Operational notes: Option B requires an uplift and may require dedicated retention configuration on their Dedicated/Private deployment. I've attached a one-sheet (redline_summary.xlsx) summarizing trade-offs.

If Acme Legal agrees to Option A we can sign and deliver the Deletion Declaration within 5 business days of termination.

On a separate note, Marcus confirmed we can provide log export capabilities and parity between hosted + private deployments; I've included the data flow diagram to show where logs are buffered and exported (data_flow_diagram.png).

If this looks OK, can Acme Legal confirm which option they'd prefer and whether they need the inclusion of "key destruction evidence" language?

Cheers,
Alex
